STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER AS TO SUGGESTED HOLIDAY.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Russell (Hon. Charles Murphy) made an inquiry in the House a few days ago. with respect to a press report that Australia had made arrangements to send 50,000 members of the original Australian Expeditionary Force to their homes for rest. I addressed a telegram on the same day to Sir George Perley in the following terms:
Press telegram reports Australia has made arrangements to send fifty thousand of original Australian Expeditionary Force home for a rest irrespective whether corresponding reinforcements are sent from Australia. Question as to this has been asked in House of Commons. Please report soon as possible whether press statement has any and what foundation.
To which I received a reply yesterday as follows:
Australian High Commissioner's office states question of returning original Australian Expeditionary Force was raised in Australian House but no instructions have come to Australian headquarters, London, regarding such return and High Commissioner's office not aware of any action taken to effectuate it.

subsubtopic: REFERENCES BY RT. HON. SIR ROBERT BORDEN AND RT. HON. SIR WILFRID LAURIER TO THE LATE COLONEL HENRY R. SMITH.
speechtext:
I
have to announce to the House, with very deep regret, that Col. Henry Robert Smith, Serjeanit-at-Arms, died this morning. The son of a distinguished Speaker of the old Parliament of Canada, he was appointed Deputy Serjeant-at-Arms in 1872 and promoted to be Serjeant-at-Arms in 1892. He has, therefore, served as deputy and as Serjeant-at-Arms for nearly half a century. Col. Smith had also a very considerable military service, in 1866 and 1872 on the frontier, and in 1885 in the Northwest Rebellion. Those of us who have known him in the course of his important official duties have, I am sure, been impressed with the dignity and courtesy with which he discharged them. He was, in a word, a fine type of a gentleman of the old school and his passing away is a distinct loss to the public life of this country. He was a man of much culture, having a very wide acquaintance with English literature, and altogether he was a most interesting personality. I am sure all the members of the House will join with me in an expression of profound sympathy to all the members of his family.

subsubtopic: REFERENCES BY RT. HON. SIR ROBERT BORDEN AND RT. HON. SIR WILFRID LAURIER TO THE LATE COLONEL HENRY R. SMITH.
speechtext: It is with as much regret as that of my right hon. friend that I learned of the sudden death of Colonel Smith. To me, personally, who am now one of the oldest members of this House, the death of Colonel Smith causes me very keen sorrow. Too much praise cannot be given to our late friend. As every hon. member knows, he was one of the best servants we ever had. He was a man of the strictest integrity, of the highest sense of honour, and of unfailing courtesy. It is not too much to say that he had endeared himself to every member of the House who had anything to do with the management of public business.

subsubtopic: RETIREMENT OF DR. FLINT, WHO BY RESOLUTION OF THE HOUSE IS ACCORDED THE PRIVILEGE OF A SEAT AT THE TABLE ON OCCASIONS OF CEREMONY.
speechtext:
An intimation has been already conveyed to the House that the Clerk of the House pur-

poses retiring from the duties of his office, which he has discharged for some fifteen years. Previous to his acceptance of the office which he now holds, Dr. Flint, had a distinguished career in Parliament' and in the public life of the country, and since he undertook the responsibilities of the important office of Clerk of the House, *all of the members who have come in contact with him have appreciated the ability, zeal, .and industry which he has uniformly displayed in the discharge of his duties.
I desire to express my own personal recognition of his uniform courtesy and his unfailing attention to all matters which I have had to bring to his notice in the ten years which I served as leader of the Opposition, and in the six years which I have had imposed upon me the responsibilities of First Minister.
I feel perfectly confident that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will join with me in proposing a resolution which I am sure will meet with universal acceptance by all the members of this House. It is my privilege to move, seconded by Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
That in view of the long- and faithful services of Doctor Thomas B. Flint, Clerk of the House of Commons, he be continued after his retirement an honorary officer of this House, and that he be allowed the entree of the House of Commons and a seat at the Table on occasions of ceremony.
Right hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that we are to lose the services of Doctor Flint, I second this motion with very great pleasure. I join cordially in everything that has been said by my right hon. friend in appreciation of the services of Doctor Flint, and I am sure that in his remarks he only expressed what is felt by everybody. Doctor Flint has been not only attentive but indefatigable in the discharge of his duties towards both parties in this House. As an old personal friend, I regret more than I can say that the condition of his health forces him to the relinquishment of the duties he has so well performed. I am sure that I reflect the feelings of all when I express the hope that his health may be restored, and that he may long be spared to move amongst us.

speechtext:
May I be permitted to draw the attention 
of the Secretary of State to something which may not have been intended in the last revision of the Franchise Act. Paragraph (g) of section 70 of the Dominion Elections Act provides that:	.
Every person accepting or holding any office, commission or employment, permanent or temporary, in the service of the Government of Canada at the nomination of the Crown or at the nomination of any of the officers of the Government of Canada,
-shall be debarred from offering himself as a candidate for the Federal House. By the Act of 1915 to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act it is provided that serving in the naval' and military forces of Canada and receiving emolument therefor shall not render a man ineligible as a member of the House of Commons. Now the question arises whether under the last revision of the Franchise Act any member or candidate to the House of Commons would be disqualified if he accepted a position on any of the tribunals and received his expenses therefor. I think that point ought to be taken into consideration, and the Act amended so ae not to disqualify any person undertaking that work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS (MADE BT THE SENATE CONCURRED IN AFTER FURTHER AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of amendments of a more or less important character have been made by the Senate to this Bill. I understand that so far as those amendments are concerned they are not likely to be of a controversial nature, provided the motion which I am now about to make should commend itself to the judgment of the House. There has been a conference with respect to those amendments between gentlemen on both sides of the House, and as the result of those conferences I now beg to move, seconded by Hon. Mr. Meighen:
That the Senate amendments to Bill No. 133 be concurred in, subject to amendment of such amendments as follow:
(a)	By striking out of paragraph 2 of subsection 5 of the new section 65A, provided by said Bill, the word "made" and inserting instead in each case the word "completed" as said word appears in lines 19 and 21 of page 1162 of Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons.
(b)	By striking out of said paragraph 2 of said subsection 5 of section 65 A provided by said Bill the words "except the issuance in any necessary case of a certificate in form W3 under paragraph (g) of section 6T," which words appear in the 33rd, 34th and 35th lines of said Votes and Proceedings.
I shall ask the Secreary of State to make any explanation that may be desired of the other amendments. So far as these were concerned, they were brought to my attention this morning by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and by my colleague from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). I think there is very good reason for the amendment because, as was pointed out to .me the use of the word "completed" gives a definite date, whereas the use of the word " made " does not give a precisely definite date under the law of Nova Scotia in respect of which this amendment is made. In regard to the other amendment, it was represented to me by the hon. gentlemen I have mentioned that, under the special provisions which are made for the province o.f .Nova Scotia, it is neither desirable nor necessary that there should be any further action by the enumerators. I concur in that view. The result of that would Ibe that those lists having been revised under judicial sanction will stand and the enumerator will have no further duty to perform with regard to them. It seemed to me that amendment was a reasonable one, and, therefore, after the conference to which I have alluded, I thought we might accept the amendments made by the Senate, with the further amendments that are em-



bodied in the resolution I have just proposed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS (MADE BT THE SENATE CONCURRED IN AFTER FURTHER AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Government would have attempted the establishment of a Federal Franchise Act applicable to every province of Canada. At least it would surely have been applied to the province of New Brunswick and to other provinces where there is not, in whole or in part, something approaching a judicial revision of the list. Only one inference can be drawn; that is that this amendment was designed for the purpose of gaining a political advantage in the province of Nova Scotia, and why that one province should be singled out for this purpose is something I cannot understand. I register my protest against it. I say we have a system of revision of lists in Nova Scotia that is as good	as that
in any other province, if not better. That revision was last completed in March last. As hon. gentlemen know, it requires a great deal of labour on the part of members of Parliament and of 4 p.m. political organizations to obtain a revision- of voters' lists annually. That list in Nova Scotia was completed but a few months ago. Nobody in my province was complaining -about the revision. I venture to say that no protest or complaint was lodged with the Government by any responsible person living in my province against that revision. I say that this amendment does not originate from anybody except the members from my province supporting the Government, and their only motive in suggesting and supporting such an amendment in the Senate and its passage through this House is a political one. In December next we shall be obliged to commence a revision of our lists again, and concurrently with the forthcoming election members of Parliament in my province will be obliged to undergo the expense, anxiety and labour of carrying on a revision of the lists, something which has never occurred before. Where the system of electoral revision by enumerators is in vogue and where that has been the practice and the established system, it may not be so objectionable; but it is objectionable to-my province, and I believe that will be the judgment of everybody in it, both Liberal and Conservative. Therefore I say it entails an unnecessary amount of labour and expense upon everybody, after having undergone, just two or three months ago, a revision of our lists, to be obliged to undergo the same thing in the course of another month or two. And what for? Just to gratify the unwholesome, the unjust, desires of some hon. gentlemen opposite. Because they think they can gain some personal and political advantage in fMr. A. Xu Maclean.]
the forthcoming election we must go through a vast amount of work and incur a considerable expense. In the end very few names will be added to the electoral lists outside of women, and very few will be struck off outside of those -struck off for reason of alienage. I venture the prediction that when this Bill becomes law and the revision takes place under this amendment, hon. gentlemen opposite who are responsible for this amendment will' regret that they ever promoted such legislation. Further than that, I -say that it adds to the burdens placed upon candidates iin this election. There is that immense soldiers' vote to be taken care of, which requires -a vast amount of organization and expense on the part of all candidates. Then we have the enfranchisement of women voters in all the provinces, and that entails vast labour and expense. One would think that that would be sufficient additional burden to throw upon candidates and party organizations in this election, without introducing this further complication at this particular moment.
I understand that this legislation is justified upon the ground that in Nova Scotia the appeal from the work of the revisers is to the sheriffs, who are political officers appointed by the Government of Nova Scotia. Complaint is made that the appeal should be heard by a judicial officer and not by -such an- officer as a sheriff. At least I have heard that presented as a justification f-o-r this amendment. I -s-ay it is not a sound reason- and will not be received as suich in the province of Nova -Scotia by any con-sider-a-ble number on either side of politics. Our lists are prepared by municipal officers who are called revisers. These revisers are appointed by the municipal councils or county councils, because the municipality practically corresponds geographically with our county lines. In some of the counties the majorities are Conservative; in other counties, it is true, the majority in the municipal council may be Liberal. Three or four years ago tRe majority of the county councils of my province were Conservative. In the constituency which I represent, the majority of the municipal council are Conservative. In the counties of Guysborough and An-tigon-isih the majorities are Conservative and the lists are made up by officers appointed by these people. I have had more or less to do necessarily diu-rimg the last twenty years in connection with the revision of lists, and I do give it to the House as my opinion and my judgment that our franchise system is

satisfactory to everybody in our province. I do not say you will not find complaints. No franchise system is capable of construction which would be satisfactory to every person. Naturally, some person of doubtful qualification or without qualification seeks enfranchisement and is refused. He complains and is dissatisfied, as probably would be the candidate seeking the enrolment of that particular name. That, however, does not prove that the franchise system is wrong, or that it is in any respect open to objection.
With respect to appeals to the sheriff, the number of appeals' in Nova Scotia in any one year is altogether a negligible quantity. I do not pretend to speak accurately, but I venture to say that in many years, particularly in years when an election is1 not likely to take place, there are practically no appeals. In my constituency, where there is an electoral list of over 20,000, only 25 appeals were .asserted by my political friends at the revision last March, fifteen of which were allowed and ten refused, I think that 25 is as large a number of appeals as is usually asserted in any year in my constituency. In the county of Annapolis this year 28 appeals were made on both sides; probably 6,000 or 7,000 voters are enrolled in that constituency. They would not tolerate that in the province of Nova Scotia the same principles of making the lists should obtain which they had themselves imposed twelve years before in regard to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. That is all that we propose, and not even that. We proposed safeguards in Alberta and Saskatchewan which never obtained before, and which, though hon. gentlemen complain of them, they did not want to have removed at ail. We had to do without those safeguards twelve years ago. Hon. gentlemen opposite were not satisfied to have Nova Scotia put in the same category as the four western provinces and Prince Edward Island, and they rose in protest. At the conference threats were made. They would not stand for Nova Scotia being put in the same class with the four western provinces, even under the safeguards then existing, and unless Nova Scotia was put back wheie it was, and the final say rested with the sheriff as of yore instead of there being the judicial revision that obtained in the four western provinces, they threatened to do so and so. That is the origin of
the legislation, be it good or be it bad. What is this legislation? What is it that all this disputing is about, and to which objection is taken? This legislation, described shortly, has this effect. It places the province of Nova Scotia in a position very similar, though not altogether the same, as the cities in the province of Ontario-very similar, let me repeat, to the cities in the province of Ontario. It provides that the list that are now in force there, shall be the basis of the lisfts that shall be made by the enumerators as the lists of that province. But those lists, so made up by the enumerators, go before the courts of that province-and I shall define the courts in a moment-for revision prior to the election.
Judicial revision in that province prior to the election is the principle of the amend-

ment to which hon. gentlemen object. Does it sound very strong logic in the mouth of the hon. member for Halifax to say: "I protest against the system embodied in this amendment, which means judicial revision of the lists-or, as he calls it, a judicial appeal of the lists-prior to the elections, and instead of. that I want appeal of the lists to stand as they are now, resting in the sheriffs alone"? What this amendment provides is in reality the substituting of the county court judiciary of the province of Nova Scotia for the sheriffs of Nova Scotia. That is what my hon. friend protests against. The women are added, and the aliens and others are struck off who are shown to have had no right to go on at the time the lists were made, any others are added who have the right to go on. The lists then come before the judges of Nova Scotia and are revised by them prior to election day. This was not made more general in this Act, because it was felt that in some rural parts of the country in particular, and in very many parts of the country not altogether rural, judicial revision was in its purest form an absolute impossibility if we were to have the election in any reasonable time. Therefore the method was confined to the province of Nova Scotia. It was suggested that to get over the difficulty the judges should do the work so far as they could, but that they should have the privilege of naming barristers of a certain number of.years' standing to conduct the revisions in other parts where they could not act, so that while the judges do not do it all themselves it is done by others named by the judges and in no way named by or appertaining to the party in power. That is the system of judicial revision which will obtain under this amendment in the province of Nova Scotia, and that is the system which we submit to the House as preferable to the system of sheriff revision which has obtained in days gone by. It is true, it was proposed to adopt lists that could be adopted at all, in so far as those lists were completed, and on that principle I submitted the Bill to the House including the Nova Scotia lists as adopted. When those matters were represented to us as they were, that Nova Scotia was not in the same position even as New Brunswick and in a much different position from the provinces Of Ontario and Quebec where there was full and complete judicial revision, it was not deemed unfair that that province should be given the advantage of judicial revision in place of sheriff revision. That is the purpose of this amend-

meat and it lias no other purpose. While hon. gentlemen opposite have a perfect right to object to the amendment, still I think the public of this country will come to the conclusion that an improvement has been made in the Act, and that there is no very great sincerity on the part of hon. members in arguing against a judicial revision in place of a sheriff revision in the province of Nova Scotia.

speechtext:
I quite understand there are people in Nova Scotia who advocate a judicial revision, and I 'am not putting myself against the proposal, but I will make the statement that there has not been any injustice done in the province of Nova Scotia so far as the sheriffs are concerned. The responsible party is not the sheriff, but the municipal council. Each county is divided up into polling districts, a group of polling districts is called a revisal district, and the municipal councillor practically appoints the reviser for his polling division. He stands up in the presence of his colleagues in the council and proposes his man as reviser for that district. If he proposes a man who is not regarded as straight and honest, his proposal will not be accepted. The practice has been so satisfactory in Nova Scotia that it is a rare thing to have an appeal. Since this proposed change was suggested, I telegraphed to my county. I received an answer yesterday from the municipal district of St. Mary's to the effect that there had not been an appeal for many years against the lists made by the revising officers. I telegraphed to the other municipality, Guysborough, and I am informed that the year before last there were no appeals; last year there were twelve. In the county of Antigonis'h, which is not part of the constituency yet, but which I hope to represent, there were no appeals last year or the year before. No one will say the reason why there were no appeals was that they did not expect to get justice from the sheriffs. The reason was because every one was perfectly satisfied with the lists made by the revisers. The Prime Minister of Nova Scotia, Hon. George H. Murray, is well known throughout Canada as a candid and truthful man. It appears he has heard of this measure going through the House. I have a message sent by him to an hon. member of this House, in which he says:
I have a general knowledge of the revision of the provincial lists in the province of Nova Scotia for a period of twenty-five years, and I have no knowledge of any objection from either of the political parties to the fairness of the decisions of the sheriffs as court of appeal. I have consulted other officials of the Government, and they are all of opinion that our

sheriffs have always acted independently and without political prejudice. Our sheriffs hold office during good behaviour. I would regard a return to the preparation of lists by partisan temporary officials on the eve of a pending election as likely to develop a great amount of bitter feeling. You must understand that our provincial system provides for every measure of publicity by the posting of lists in public places, and ample opportunity is given both parties for every reasonable objection.
That, Sir, is the statement of the Premier of Nova Scotia who is known by every hon. member on both sides of this House to be an honourable and fair man and one who knows what he is talking about. The municipal councils are the responsible bodies and we propose to pass an Act which will cast a reflection not only upon the sheriffs but upon every municipal council in Nova Scotia. The conduct of the sheriffs has been been criticised by hen. gentlemen who have spoken but the Prime Minister himself has given a certificate of character to the late sheriff of Halifax, Mr. Donald Archibald. He said that he regarded him as a fair man. He was for many years sheriff of that county. He also stated the other day that the present sheriff of Halifax was regarded as a fair man so there has been no complaint in Halifax. I can say the same thing for the sheriff of Pictou There is no man who knows him who would venture to say that he would be guilty of any unfairness in regard to the revision of the lists. The same can be said of the sheriffs of Antigonish, Guysborough and Colchester. These are the sheriffs whom T know best. The statement that this amendment becomes necessary in order to avoid injustice on the part of the sheriffs of Nova Scotia is not well founded and cannot be supported by evidence.
Why does the Secretary of State depart from the policy that he laid down when this Bill was introdtieed? We all understood that the policy of the Government with regard to the four provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec was that the existing lists were to hold and that no changes were to be made except those that were necessary to add the names of female relatives of soldiers and to strike off the names of aliens. That was the policy laid down by the Secretary of State for those four provinces. What justification can there be for singling out the province of Nova Scotia and adopting a different system. The only possible explanation is that it was done for the sake of obtaining a partisan advantage for the Conservative side. This is what the Secretary of State said when introducing the Bill. 
The lists so made up of male voters all judicially revised in Ontario and Quebec and revised by the provincial methods in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, are by this Bill adopted, so far as they go. The only requirement as to them is to add such of the women as toy this Bill are to be entitled to vote and to substract such of the men, if any, as, by reason of alienage, should not toe entitled to vote.
Then he goes on to say:
As regards these latter the lists are adopted and the enumeration only goes to the adding of the names of the additional women now entitled to vote and to the striking off of those who by reason of alienage, and nothing else, are disentitled to vote. That is the province and duty of the registrars or enumerators, whatever you call them, and that alone.
Why was not that principle followed out in Nova Scotia? It was simply for the reason that the Nova Scotia members of the Conservative side asked that this change be made in order to load the dice and gain a partisan advantage. That is the only reason that can be given. Under the provincial law of Nova Scotia practically every man who is entitled to a vote becomes an elector. The requirements are very low. The ownership of $150 worth of real estate entitles a man to vote. If he earns $250 he is entitled to be placed on the register as an income voter. If he owns a farm worth $600 he can qualify himself and four sons. Practically every man in Nova Scotia who desires a vote has it under the existing system. The county councils are primarily responsible and they discharge the duty well.
The Government propose by this amendment to adopt a system which is altogether different. The enumerators are appointed by themselves and are practically certain to be partisans. They will all be of one stripe. You cannot have that in the county councils. County councils and revisers appointed by them are bound to be composed or men of both political parties, sometimes Conservative and sometimes Liberal. In the county which I have the honour to represent the county council happens for the last term to be Conservatives, but I have no reason to complain in regard to their action in apointing revisers for making lists. Under this proposal the partisan enumerator does not even require to be a resident of the district. A stranger who never saw the district, and who is not known to a single inhabitant in the district may be sent in to act as enumerator.
If permitted I would like to make an appeal to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is going to ask the people of Can-

ada for re-election, in a few weeks. He will issue a manifesto. In. that manifesto there will he a paragraph stating that he has made every effort to obtain a Union Government. He will ask the Canadian people to cast aside all partisanship and to unite with him, in helping to push forward the great enterprise that we all have so much at heart. That will no doubt be a part of his appeal to the people. But the people will ask him a (question and that question will be: "Did you forget partisanship yourself?" Let me say this, ,Mr. Speaker: the very last act of his Administration will be regarded by every liberal and fair-minded man in Nova Scotia as a piece of extreme partisanship and it will not read very well side by side with the manifesto which my right hon. friend will issue. If I had a right to make a proposal to him it would be this: Refuse to agree to this amendment of the Senate and leave the lists in Nova Scotia alone, except to add the names of the female relatives of soldiers and to 6trike out the names of aliens. Say to the Senate that it is no part of their duty to interfere with the lists for election of members of the House of Commons. Let the Prime Minister say to the hon. members for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) the hon. member for Queens aud Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) the hon. gentleman in the other chamber from Pictou Mr. John C. Douglas of Oape Breton, and all the other gentlemen who are pressing the Government in this matter that they must go back to their counties and win their elections in fair fight on the lists that are in existence now and as they have been fairly made by the municipal councils in Nova Scotia. I suppose my right hon. friend will not take my advice but it is my duty to offer it to him and it is my duty to protest with all the energy I have against this attempt to bedevil the electoral lists of my province and thereby gain a partisan advantage for the Conservative party in Nova Scotia.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Electoral Franchise Act of Nova Scotia was based upon the Municipal Incorporations Act passed in 1879 under the auspices of the only Conservative Government that ever existed in Nova Scotia since Confederation. The Holmes-Thompson Government, in the first session after its accession to office, passed the Municipal Incorporation Act which established the county councils and made provision for the appointment of revisers to prepare the voters' lists at each annual meeting of these municipal councils. These revisers are appointed according to the political complexion of the councillor representing each polling district. Every municipal council is made up of councillors of both political parties and it is a fact that no matter what may be the political complexion of the majority of the councillors a Conservative councillor always has the right to nominate his own reviser.

speechtext:
I suppose there is no man
in public life who has more information that is not true than the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson). I repeat that the revisers are appointed upon the nomination of Conservative councillors irrespective of whether the majority of the councillors is Liberal or Conservative.
That being the case, there is always a large number of Conservative revisers appointed in Nova Scotia. In the municipality of the county which I represent, there is a-majority of Conservative councillors, and the majority of revisers in that county is also Conservative. In the town in which I live, the three revisers are Conservatives. They held a revision of the electoral list on the fifth of March last, and after they had heard applications involving the adding to or striking off from the list of 25 or 30 names, only one appeal was taken to the sheriff of the county. In the municipality of the county of Cape Breton, where there are some 20,000 votes, the revisers held their court on the 5th of March last, and although they considered hundreds and perhaps thousands of applications to be added to or rejected from the voters' lists, not a single appeal was taken to the sheriff of the county of Cape Breton. I do not think that even the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) will undertake to say that the people of Cape Breton, whether Liberal or Conservative, have not confidence in Mr. George B. Ingraham, sheriff of the county. It is no answer to the statement I make that no appeals were taken to the sheriff last year to say that the people had not confidence in Sheriff Ingraham.

speechtext: Who would be better able to say that than Judge-

speechtext:
If any person weie rash
enough to make that statement it would be indignantly denied by every one in

Nova Scotia who knows Sheriff Ingraham. But so fair was the revision, so eminently satisfactory was the work performed by the revisers in the various municipal districts, as well as by the registrar of voters in Sydney and Glace Bay, that every person was perfectly satisfied with the revision of the lists. The same thing is true of every county in eastern Nova Scotia. I cannot undertake to say what are the conditions in western Nova Scotia, but the onjy criticism that has been directed against the .appeals carried to sheriffs in Nova Scotia was the one case referred to by the hon. member for Annapolis, I do not know what conditions exist in Annapolis, but, judging from the choice of the electors of that county as witnessed by the present representative, I should say the electorate of that county does strange things on occasions. The point made by the Secretary of State (Mr. 5 p.m. Meighen) that this amendment had to be added in the Senate because there was no opportunity of doing so here, cannot prevail with members of this House, who know the circumstances so well. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) read from the speech made by the Secretary of State when introducing this Bill in which he said it was proposed to adhere to the lists in the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec. If, when this Bill was going through the House of Commons, it was intended by the Secretary of	State or by the
Prime Minister to make the changes that were afterwards made by the other body of this Parliament, surely the Secretary of State would not have committed himself to the principle that the lists in the province of Nova Scotia would prevail. The fact that the Secretary of State made that statement to the House of Commons is proof positive that no such change in the basis of the electoral lists in the province of Nova Scotia was in contemplation. The fact of the matter is that when this Bill got over to the Senate there was unusual activity on the part of certain hon. gentlemen representing constituencies in Nova Scotia who support this Government. Not only were they exercised as to the form and shape in which this franchise Bill should go back to the electors of Nova Scotia, and not only were they exercised themselves, but the assistance of certain other gentlemen who do not at the present time hold seats in this House was called upon. There was present in their conferences a gentleman prominent in public affairs in Cape

Breton for some years, who has exercised a most (baleful influence upon the public life of eastern Nova Scotia. That gentleman was in consultation with members supporting the Government in this House from day to day, and as a result of their combined wisdom, they came to the conclusion that the only chance they had of carrying the province of Nova Scotia was by loading the dice and imposing a franchise on the people of Nova Scotia that would give them an undue advantage. There is no gainsaying that. There is no other argument that can be urged which will meet the case. The result of the amendment that is being proposed by the other body of this Parliament is to deprive the workingmen of the large centres in the county of Cape Breton of their franchise. We have, as is well known, a large population engaged in industrial occupations in that constituency. In addition to the 6,000 men employed in the steel works at Sydney and Sydney Mines, there are 7,000 or 8,000 employees in the collieries of the Dominion Coal Company and the Nova Scotia Coal Company. These men exercise a large influence in public affairs in eastern Nova Scotia at the present time. The result of the voting upon the issues which will be submitted to these people in the present election is viewed with a good deal of apprehension by hon. gentlemen opposite and is greatly feared by the gentlemen who will be the candidates of the Government in the ensuing election. It is pretty well known that the labouring men throughout the country are opposed to this Government. They are opposed to this Government, not only on the subject of conscription but because the, Government has failed, when conscripting men, to conscript the wealth of this country as well. The workingmen of Cape Breton aTe opposed to this Government because the Government has failed to grapple with the great question of the cost of living. The working people of Canada realize that, while sacrifices are being demanded of men who are asked to recruit for overseas service and to give up their lives in the cause of the Allies and in defence of the principles of liberty, the sacrifice has been limited almost entirely to the men who enlist for overseas service, and that instead of sacrifices being made by men engaged in industrial enterprise in Canada, many of these men have taken the opportunity which the war gave them of amassing large fortunes. These are some of the reasons why the working people in Canada, and moTe particularly in the

island of Cape Breton, are opposed to this Government .
Hon. gentlemen who desire the Government to win constituencies in Nova Scotia and who realize that the sentiment of the working people is against them in this contest determined when this Franchise Bill went over to the other House of this Parliament, that they would introduce an amendment to the franchise which would result in disfranchising a large element of the population in the industrial centres of Nova Scotia and placing upon the electoral list a large number who are not qualified and would not otherwise be placed upon it. No person will realize that better than the workingmen themselves, and none will be readier to respond to the appeals for justice and fair play which will be made to them when the election comes in the course of the next few weeks. We in Nova Scotia have been singled out for special treatment by this Government. The electoral lists of New Brunswick are to stand as the basis of the franchise to be used in the coming election. The electoral lists in Ontario and Quebec are to stand as the basis of the franchise for the coming election. But the province of Nova Scotia-and I regret to have to say it, the province represented by the right hon. the Prime Minister-has been singled out for unfair treatment in order that this Government may get an unfair advantage when it comes to the elections in that province, the result of which they fear so greatly.
I should feel that I was not discharging my full duty to the people whom I represent in the island of Cape Breton if I did not make as strenuous a protest as I am capable of making against this iniquitous legislation, which was designed solely and exclusively to steal the election for the Government in Nova Scotia.

Mr. Speaker, my observation of
discussions in this Parliament has not led me to the conclusion that condemnation by hon. members opposite of any proposed measure carries with it any assurance that that measure is without merit. The strenuous opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite to the Senate amendment of itself suggests to one's mind that there may be something wrong with the present lists.
I have talked with many members of the House from western Canada, where the systemensuring fresh lists pr evails. I listened to the discussions in this House of the Wartime Elections Bill and I failed to hear any objection or any criticism of the manner in which the enumerator system operates in the western provinces. Personally I should have preferred the extension of that system to Nova Scotia. It already applies to Prince Edward Island. I should have liked to see it in operation in Nova Scotia, but as a result of conferences which took place between hon. gentlemen opposite and Liberal members of the Senate, instead of having a uniform system for Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as was proposed originally in the Senate we are now to have a system which applies to Nova Scotia only.
I cannot follow the argument of the member foT Richmond (Mr. Kyte) when he says that men will be unfairly disqualified by this amendment. He has failed to point out any unfairness in this provision or shown how it will work to the disadvantage of any portion of the electorate. Surely no hardship can result through enlarging the opportunity to correct previous errors and wrongs. Under the system which has prevailed in Nova Scotia, good Canadians have frequently been left off the list. Under normal conditions the average citizen is not much concerned about having his name added to the voters' list, and a great deal of care and attention is necessary to see that he is registered. Under the old system a person fully qualified to be registered would find his name omitted from the lists.
At this crisis, when the people are to pass upon an issue of utmost national importance every patriotic citizen should have the opportunity of voting. Every opportunity should be given for bringing the lists up to date. This is not a case where voters are endeavouring to get their names on the lists; rather it is an occasion where the greatness of the issue demands the expression of every loyal man's opinion.
Had no amendment been made to the Bill, if the name of a man was not on the provincial list last revised, he would be denied the right to vote. Every member from Nova Scotia knows of cases where people properly entitled to the vote have had their names left off the list. In some counties of Nova Scotia the lists contain thousands of names with no addresses at all; these names may or may not be fictitious.

In any business concern that is honestly 'managed and where fair dealing is desired, there is never any objection to audit or revision. subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY THE DIRECTOR GENERAL, MR. R. B. BENNETT.
speechtext:
Perhaps, before the House arises, I might avail myself of this opportunity to state that now that the Military Service Act has come into force and various Orders in Council have oeen passed, dealing with matters which have received the attention of the National Service Board, this organization has ceased to exist. The various directors have tend red their resignations which have been placed in the hands of the Government. I tendered my resignation on the introduction of the Military Service Act. I came into the position under very peculiar circumstances, and it might not be amiss if I stated them shortly. In September of last year I received a telegram asking me if I would act as Director of National Service for the province in which I resided. I agreed to do so if I could be of any service to my country. I came to Ottawa in October in response to a call issued by Sir Thomas Tait, Director General of National Service, for a meeting of the district directors. I attended the meetings on the second day of the conference. On the next day, Sir Thomas Tait resigned, and it was necessary to appoint a successor. I was asked to accept the position. I did so with very great reluctance, believing, as I did, that I should not accept that responsibility, having regard to the conditions that prevailed. But if I may be permitted to use the language of Mr. Neville Chamberlain,

who accepted a somewhat similar post under somewhat similar circumstances, I was impressed by the fact, perhaps improperly, by those who urged me, that it was a patriotic duty on my part to undertake this work, and I accordingly did so. I have no regret to offer except to indicate that, at that time, the policy of the bo rd had been settled and the question as to what the general duties were had been fixed by Orders in Council. Those orders contemplated largely that the work should be carried on by district directors and not from Ottawa, but owing to difficulties that arose at the very inception of the work, it became necessary that the largest part of the work should be carried on in Ottawa. We undertook the work and endeavoured to discharge the responsibility as best we could.
At the initial meeting which was held here and to which I have referred a resolution was passed that a man-power inventory should be taken and that the signing of cards which were sent out should be compulsory, and that a penalty should be provided for their not being signed. The resolution, which was passed before Sir Thomas Tait resigned was very explicit upon that point. Those in authority, however, thought that could not be done, and, we were compelled to endeavour as best we could to create an atmosphere sufficient to induce the people voluntarily to- sign the cards. In order to create that atmosphere, letters were sent to members of Parliament, senators, members of the local legislatures, labour unions, clergymen, boards of trade, fraternal organizations and practically 150,000 representative men throughout the country. Public meetings were held, advertisements were inserted in the newspapers and the first week of the year was proclaimed National Service Week. It is only fair to say that the response was much better than might reasonably have been expected, and one would hesitate to describe, except in the warmest terms, the spirit of co-operation and sympathy displayed by all those who were appealed to at this time. The result was that, by this voluntary effort, a very large number of cards were signed and returned. I ventured to point out at that time in public addresses, that this was the last great voluntary effort on the part of the Government, and the response as I have said, was everything that could be expected. The time for filling in cards was extended, but no penalty was provided and the Government did not think it advisable to make 385
it obligatory to complete the cards. It is highly important, nay, absolutely necessary that there should be at all times created and maintained in this country a proper atmosphere in relation to this great conflict. That atmosphere can only be obtained by appealing, through concrete means to the sentiment and reason of the people. It was believed that the carrying on of a campaign of thrift, a campaign in relation to the saving of money and food and other matters of that kind would have the desired result. I urged when the enthusiasm of the people was apparent that a general campaign of this character should be organized and vigorously prosecuted. Eor reasons best known to those in authority the matter was not taken up at that time, but it was taken up later on. The results have to some extent justified the effort, late though it was. The enthusiasm of the people by that time had in some measure waned. When the cards came in arrangements were made to classify them, and the classification was carried on in a most comprehensive manner. I fancy perhaps very., few people have an adequate appreciation of the work that was done. That part of the work was in charge of a young lady who is a graduate of Toronto University, and also of one of the largest universities in Chicago. I refer to Miss Grange, who undertook and carried on that work successfully. The cards were divided into military prospects and industrial prospects. If the information thus obtained and still being obtained is properly collated and classified, it will assist those, who are charged with responsibility with respect to demobilization, to determine what should be done to meet a situation that, in my judgment, will be the .most acute with which the country has ever been confronted. The occupational survey will indicate the probable opportunities for work throughout Canada; the overseas cards will indi-ate what the peculiar fitness of each returning soldier may be for the work that will offer:
With the cessation of industrial activity, the result of the shutting down of munitions factories, and with the returning to these shores of three or four hundred thousand men, i:t is obvious that there will be a great displacement of woman labour, and a very great demand for employment which will not be forthcoming. One might say without being tedious, that the great problem that must confront this country is the problem that will arise when this conflict is over. The absorption into our civil life of those out of employment, as well as of those who come back, is a matter of extreme importance. The taking care of the adverse balance of trade in this country, the making provision for meeting the enormous charges upon our resources, with respect to interest both on our national debt and pensions, are matters of pressing importance. There is only one way by which that can be done, and that is by the creation of new wealth, and new wealth can only be created by increased production and the development of our vast natural resources. So it is of paramount importance that the great natural resources should be developed, and we must learn what is the desire and intention of those who are left and of those who are coming back with respect- to agriculture and other pursuits.
The great problem this State will have to deal with is the problem of how adequately to- encourage production and development. With the burden of taxation the people will have to bear, it is only necessary to say that new capital will not come here as willingly as some people seem to think. The great problem is how to induce capital to find here an opportunity for profitable employment while at the same time arranging that adequate provision is made for the state receiving its share of the profits that may result from any enterprise that utilizes our natural resources which the state holds as trustee for all the people. I shall not dwell longer on that point. I have not time this afternoon to do more than indicate the activities that have been undertaken by the board with respect to farm labour and increased grain production during the present year, the providing of men for specific undertakings, the Royal Flying Corps, railway, shipbuilding and many other pursuits, the advertising campaign for thrift and war savings. All these things we have endeavoured to do as best we could, with what degree of success it is not for me at the present moment to discuss. In my judgment, however, the language used by Mr. Chamberlin, the Director General of National Service in England, in dealing with similar conditions might aptly apply here. He said:
It is apparent that the rock upon which the department split was the fact that a local habitation and a loud sounding name were given to it, and that it was then launched with a roving commission to discover its functions and duties, but left without any statutory powers and no boundaries delimiting its sphere from that of other departments. My reluctance to accept such a vaguely defined post was natural, hut I accepted from patriotic motives and have done my best.
I think the language of Mr. Chamberlin's valedictory might well be the language 1 should employ as mine, and in so doing 1 desire to thank the press for the very great effort they have made at all times,

under difficult circumstances to insure so far as possible the success of the movement. The thanks of this country are due to the district directors who earnestly and sincerely laboured to make their work a success and particularly to Mr. C. W. Paterson the unpaid secretary of the board to whose zeal, patience, persistence and energy in no small degree the success of the work that was undertaken is due. Nothing, however, could have left with me a mere lasting or a more pleasant memory than the recollection of the sympathy which all who are in this House have extended to me in the work I was unfortunate enough to have been induced to undertake. I shall never forget the kindliness of their criticism, and their willingness to appreciate and understand the difficulties under which the work was carried on.

There is some difference, on this side of the House at any rate, as to whether an elector who is on the voters' list of the province of Ontario, who has left the electoral district, is entitled to vote. Section 32 of the Wartime Elections Act, provides that:
The qualifications necessary to enable any male person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as by this Act otherwise provided, he those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such male person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
Under the law of the province of Ontario a male person, in order to vote, has to be a resident on the day of polling domiciled in the district in which he is voting. I should like to- ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) whether that rule will still prevail under this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can only give my opinion of the interpretation of the provisions of the Ac-t, but I am very clear in that opinion. Under the first paragraph of section 32, it is made quite clear that the qualifications to vote, prescribed by -the law of any province are to be the qualifications of male voters under this Act, save in so far -as they may be modified by the provisions of - this Act. There are but two provisions which I have heard it suggested might be said to modify' what I understand to be the requirements of the Ontario law, that in order to be enr titled to vote a person must be a resident in the constituency at the time he voted. The two provisions that have been suggested as possibly modifying that are subsection 2 of section 32 and section 143.

As regards subsection 2, a perusal of it will make it perfectly clear, I think, that it deals with the subject of residence only from the point of view of the operation of preparing or adding to the lists. Its purpose is merely to fix -a date in relation to which the period of time required in any province for residence within the province and for residence within the constituency, shall be fixed, and it fixes the period of residence essential to entitle a man to be placed upon the list as one year within the provinces, as I understand the amendment of the Senate, and thirty days within the constituency, such periods to be fixed by reference ot the date of the writ of election. That d-eal-s only with the question of residence so far as it is to be considered in preparing or adding to lists, and its purpose and effect are merely to determine the period, and the date in relation to which that period shall be fixed.
Section 143, as I read it, is intended to-, and does, simply determine, not what is the qualification to vote, but the place at which a person having all the qualifications to vote shall be entitled to vote, and the only place at which he shall be entitled to vote. The section provides:
Except as otherwise provided in this Act, each elector shall be entitled to vote at the polling station of the polling division, or of one of the polling divisions, upon the list of voters for which his name is-*
There is a misprint in the Bill, but at all events the man's name figures on the list. I would point out that the section does not create the right to vote, -and I say that, because it deals only with a" person who is an elector, and the definition section of the Elections Act defines an elector as a person who is entitled -to vote. So that it means simply that any person- entitled to vote shall be so entitled at a particular time.

In connection with the subject under discussion, I would like to put a concrete case before the minister in order to have his judicial opinion on it. I take it for granted from what he has stated that under the provisions of section. 143 a man can only vote at the- place from which his name is upon the voters' list. According to the laws of the province of New Brunswick a man can only vote at that place in which he is a resident, but we have a very s-imple provision by which, if a man's name is properly added to the list, say in the city of St. .John, and he moved before the election to, say, the city of Moncton, his- name could be easily transferred from the list for the city of St. John to

that for the city of Moncton, and he would vote in the city of Moncton. Would the minister think that section 143 would override the provisions of our Act as to residence and the right of a man to have his name transferred from his former residence tc his present residence?

Mr. Speaker, His Excellency, the Governor General, desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the Chamber of the honourable the Senate.

Then the hon. the Speaker of the House of Commons addressed His Excellency the Governor General as follows:
May it please Your Excellency:
The Commons of Canada have voted the Supplies required to enable the Government to defray the expenses of the Public Service.
In the name of the Commons, I1 present to Your Excellency the following Bills:-
"An Act for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service of the financial year ending the 31st March, 1918.
An Act for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service of the financial year ending the 31st March, 1918." to which Bills I humbly request Your Excellency's assent.
To -these Bills the Clerk of the Senate by command of His Excellency the Governor General did thereupon say:
In His Majesty's name, His Excellency the Governor General thanks His Loyal Subjects, accepts their benevolence, and assents to these Bills.
After which His Excellency the Governor General was pleased to close the Seventh Session of the Twelfth Parliament of the Dominion with the following Speech:
Honourable Gentlemen of the Senate:
Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
Important measures for the effective prosecution of the war have engaged your close attention during a long session, and I am now happy to release you from further attendance.
Since your labours began, the high and worthy character of our cause has been confirmed by two significant events. Our allies,

the Russian people, are engaged under trying circumstances, in establishing institutions which shall fully conform to their ideals of liberty and order. In the anidst of inevitable difficulties, which command our sympathy, they have affirmed their determination to remain faithful to the Alliance.
The United States of America, refusing to tolerate the arrogance and menace of Prussian Militarism have made common cause with the Allies and are vigorously .co-operating in the struggle for freedom and humanity. Already the Canadian people have given many expressions of the warm welcome with which they greet their great kindred neighbour as a comrade in arms.
The meetings of the Imperial War Cabinet and Imperial War Conference in the early part of the year have very materially facilitated the thorough co-operation of the Dominion, both in the prosecution of the war and in preparation for the future. They constitute also an important step in the development of constitutional relationships between the nations of the British Commonwealth.
Notwithstanding the increasing military strength of the allied nations, the stubborn resistance of the enemy in all important theatres of the war demonstrates the need of throwing our utmost effort into the struggle and thus hastening the day of abiding peace. In the western theatre the Canadian Army Corps, by its capture of the coveted Vimy Ridge and by its recent operations at Lens, has sustained its distinguished record and contributed in important measure to the ascendancy which the Allies have gained in that theatre.
In order to secure the reinforcements essential for the support of our forces further steps have become necessary, and the authority you have granted for compulsory military enlistment on a selective basis will meet the urgent need for reinforcements. At the same time it will provide the means for conserving more effectively the essential agricultural *hnd industrial activities of the Dominion.
You have recognized your duty in providing the best possible safeguards for enabling those engaged in the defence of their country to have their voice in the decision of national questions which vitally affect them. For this purpose, as
well as to give due recognition to service and sacrifice in the affairs of the State, the necessary adjustments which you have made in the legislation relevant to these matters will doubtless prove effective.
The legislation you have passed for the purpose of assisting returned soldiers to settle upon the land will not only aid materially in restoring these gallant men to their rightful status in the community but should greatly increase the agricultural production of the country.
The appointment of a Food Controller and of a Fuel Controller invested with important powers and duties is founded upon the impressive need of the utmost economy and saving in order that our national strength may continue unimpaired.
In order that our industries may be equipped to cope with the intricate problems of the future, provision has been wisely made for promoting scientific and industrial research.
Important progress has been made in solving our difficult problems of railway transportation, and the means have been provided whereby a great railway system shall become the property of the people of Canada and be added to their national undertakings;
Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
In the name of His Majesty I thank you for the liberal provision you have made for the needs of the public service and for the prosecution of the war.
HouHourable Gentlemen of the Senate:
Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
Although the stress of the War becomes increasingly severe, the people of Canada, resolute in the supreme purpose of achieving through victory an abiding peace, have not faltered; and I am confident that whatever further efforts are necessary will be unhesitatingly put forth in the stern determination that the vast sacrifices already made shall not be in vain.
The Speaker of the Senate then said:
It is His Excellency the Governor General's will and pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued until Thursday, the 1st day of November next, to be here holden, and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued until Thursday, the 1st day of November next.
